body: APQ3 (average absolute difference of amplitude) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the average absolute difference of the per-cycle amplitude between consecutive glottal cycles in a voiced speech signal. For N consecutive glottal cycles with amplitudes A_i, the perturbation is computed as APQ3 = (1/(3N)) * Σ_i |A_{i+1} - A_i| / ((1/N) * Σ_i A_i), reported in percent or in dB (20*log10(std/mean)). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle amplitude measure (peak or RMS). Small APQ3 indicates amplitude stability (normal phonation); large APQ3 indicates amplitude instability (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software (Praat, laryngology toolkits) from pitch-synchronous amplitude tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment. e.g.: Praat's shimmer analysis reporting the APQ3 value; the Kay Bolt Multi-Dimensional Voice Analysis software displaying APQ3 in its voice-quality report | not: shimmer (the general category of amplitude perturbation, not the specific APQ3 computation); jitter (a period perturbation parameter, not an amplitude perturbation) [formal: scintillatio quotiens media absoluta | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

High-speed videolaryngoscopy (HSV) is a clinical imaging technique that records the vocal folds at true real-time frame rates (typically 2000-10000 frames per second) using a high-speed camera integrated into a laryngoscope. Unlike stroboscopy, HSV captures the actual motion of the vocal folds without requiring periodic or stable vibration, making it suitable for assessing irregular, aperiodic, or non-stationary phonation. Parameters: (1) the frame rate — typically 2000 to 10000 fps to capture the full vibratory cycle without aliasing, (2) the illumination — coherent white light or near-infrared source coupled through the laryngoscope, (3) the recording system — high-speed camera with buffer memory storing thousands of frames. It persists as a maintained clinical instrument: the Phox high-speed videolaryngoscopy system (PhonoVision), documented in clinical voice assessment literature. e.g.: the Phox high-speed videolaryngoscopy system by PhonoVision used in voice clinics; the HSV protocol described in Zeitels et al. at Massachusetts Eye and Ear | not: stroboscopy, which creates a slow-motion illusion from synchronized flashes rather than recording actual vibration [formal: photographia velocissima laryngoscopia | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

For a frequency band defined by lower and upper bounds [f_low, f_high) and a spectral decomposition with N frequency bins indexed i=1..N, each with a complex amplitude A_i and frequency f_i where f_low <= f_i < f_high: the distribution is the ordered vector v = (|A_1|^2, |A_2|^2, ..., |A_N|^2), where |A_i|^2 is the energy of bin i. The parameters are the band bounds and the spectral decomposition method. The persistence mechanism is the explicit storage of the N-tuple of non-negative scalars ordered by bin index. [formal: the mathematical representation | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral sequence is an ordered array of cepstral coefficients indexed by coefficient position, representing signal characteristics in the cepstral domain. Parameters: (1) number of coefficients N (typically 12-20 for speech), (2) coefficient type — filterbank-based MFCC, DFT-based, or DCT-based cepstral coefficients, (3) normalization method — mean-normalized, variance-normalized, or raw. The persistence mechanism maps (coefficient type, count, normalization) to a fixed-length vector c[1..N] where each element c[i] represents the i-th cepstral coefficient. [formal: cepstrum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Nasalance-score is an aerodynamic measure quantifying the ratio of acoustic energy radiated through the nasal port to total acoustic energy during speech, expressed as a percentage. Parameters: (1) the nasal microphone — captures acoustic energy radiated through the nostrils; (2) the oral microphone — captures acoustic energy radiated from the lips; (3) the nasalance computation — percentage = 100 * nasal_mic_energy / (nasal_mic_energy + oral_mic_energy); (4) the speech stimuli — a set of oral-dominant words (e.g., 'happy,' 'puppy') and nasal-dominant words (e.g., 'mummy,' 'bunny') that establish baseline oral and nasal nasalance values. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical protocol documented in speech-language pathology literature, implemented in NASOMETER equipment by Kay PENTAX, used in clinical voice and speech assessment, and maintained as a standard measure of velopharyngeal function. e.g.: NASOMETER oral nasalance of 12% measured in a typical speaker reading oral words; nasalance of 55% measured in a patient with cleft palate and velopharyngeal insufficiency; baseline nasal nasalance of 72% established on nasal words in a speech assessment protocol | not: GRBAS rating of breathiness, which is a perceptual dimension not an aerodynamic measurement; nasopharyngoscopy, which directly visualizes velopharyngeal closure rather than measuring acoustic output [formal: gradus nasalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

Jitter (period perturbation) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the cycle-to-cycle variation of the fundamental period in a voiced speech signal. For N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, the perturbation is computed as APQ1 = (1/(N-1)) * Σ_i |P_{i+1} - P_i| / ((1/N) * Σ_i P_i), or equivalently the standard deviation of the periods divided by their mean, reported in percent or in absolute units (milliseconds or seconds). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle period measure, (3) the perturbation variant (APQ1 — average absolute difference, JRR — ratio, JDP — absolute difference). Small jitter indicates period stability (normal phonation); large jitter indicates period instability (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software (Praat, laryngology toolkits) from pitch-synchronous period tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment. [formal: titubatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

The aryepiglottic fold is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired mucosal folds extending from the lateral margins of the epiglottis to the apex of each arytenoid cartilage, forming the superior and lateral boundaries of the laryngeal inlet and containing elastic cartilage within its substance. Parameters: (1) the mucosal surface — smooth mucosa continuous with the laryngeal vestibule, forming a visible ridge on endoscopy; (2) the contained cartilage — the corniculate cartilage at the apex of each fold and the cuneiform cartilage embedded within the fold's substance (not present in all individuals); (3) the sensory function — the fold's mucosa contains sensory endings that trigger the cough reflex when stimulated; (4) the sphincteric mechanism — the fold contributes to the sphincteric closure of the laryngeal inlet during swallowing and airway protection. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in laryngology atlases, emergency airway management protocols, and endoscopy references. e.g.: the aryepiglottic fold as the lateral boundary of the laryngeal inlet on fiberoptic laryngoscopy; the aryepiglottic fold containing the cuneiform cartilage described in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the aryepiglottic pleats palpated during digital examination for epiglottitis | not: the aryepiglottic ligament (the elastic cartilage core without the overlying mucosa, not the complete fold); the pyriform fossa (the mucosal depression lateral to the aryepiglottic fold, a separate space) [formal: plicae aryepiglotticae | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Glottal contact is the physical contact between the vocal folds during the glottal cycle, comprising the closed phase (folds in contact) and the transition phases (closing and opening). It is the spatial/physical phenomenon of vocal-fold apposition that, when modulated by subglottal pressure, generates the periodic airflow excitation of phonation. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0, glottal contact is partitioned into the contact interval (folds touching) and the non-contact interval (glottis open). Its parameters include the contact quotient (from the electroglottogram envelope) and the open quotient (ratio of open-phase duration to the period). It persists as a standardized physiological construct in speech science and clinical laryngology, measured by electroglottography and videostroboscopy. [formal: contactus glottidis | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Amplitude perturbation is a class of voice-quality parameters that quantify the cycle-to-cycle variation in the amplitude (energy level) of voiced speech. The general measure computes the normalized difference between consecutive cycle amplitudes: given N consecutive glottal cycles with amplitudes A_i, perturbation = normalized deviation of |A_{i+1} - A_i| relative to the mean amplitude. Named variants include: APQ3 (average absolute difference quotient over 3-cycle windows) and the standard deviation variant (standard deviation of cycle amplitudes divided by their mean). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal, (2) the pitch-synchronous segmentation at cycle boundaries, (3) the specific perturbation variant formula. Reported in percent or decibels (20*log10(std/mean)). Persistence mechanism: maintained as a measurement class by the discipline of laryngology and speech science; implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), taught in voice-disorder curricula, and standardized in clinical practice. [formal: perturbatio amplitude | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A spectral moment is a quantitative descriptor obtained by weighting each frequency bin of a spectral energy distribution by a power of its center frequency and summing across all bins. The n-th spectral moment is mu_n = sum_i (f_i^n * E_i) where f_i is the center frequency of bin i and E_i is the spectral energy in that bin. The zeroth moment yields total spectral energy; the first moment yields the energy-weighted mean frequency; the second central moment yields variance; higher moments characterize asymmetry (skewness) and tail heaviness (kurtosis). The construct persists as a parameterized computational routine implementable in software or hardware, standardized across audio analysis toolkits and music information retrieval systems. [formal: spectral_moment | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A Kaiser window is a parameterized family of window functions defined by the zeroth-order modified Bessel function. Its formula is: w(n) = I₀(πβ√(1−((2n−(N−1))/(N))²)) / I₀(πβ) for 0 ≤ n ≤ N−1, where I₀ is the zeroth-order modified Bessel function of the first kind, N is the window length, and β is the shape parameter. The β parameter controls the tradeoff between main-lobe width and side-lobe attenuation: β = 0 yields a rectangular window; β = 2.43 is optimal for DFT analysis; β = 3.44 approximates a Hamming window; β = 5 gives ≈−43 dB side lobes; β = 6 gives ≈−47 dB; β ≥ 9 approaches the Blackman-Harris form. The family is designed to achieve the maximum main-lobe concentration for a given side-lobe level — optimal for a specified side-lobe constraint. Persistence mechanism: the Bessel-function formula codified in DSP literature and implemented in all major signal-processing toolkits. [formal: fenestra kaißer | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.5]

Pressed voice (hyperfunctional phonation) is a classification category for a mode of phonation defined by a specific glottal configuration: the vocal folds are adducted with heavy medial contact under elevated subglottal pressure, vibrating with a short open phase and a long closed phase relative to the modal cycle, producing a tight, strained, rough timbre with elevated pitch. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration - heavy medial fold contact and elevated subglottal pressure, (2) the cycle signature - prolonged glottal closure, reduced open-phase fraction (a low open quotient) at an f0 at or above the modal range, (3) the acoustic signature - a tight, strained, rough timbre with strong low-order harmonics and increased aperiodicity from the hard glottal impact. It persists as a named mode of the phonation-mode taxonomy: documented in laryngology and phonetics, used in voice-disorder assessment (pressed voice as the hyperfunctional voice quality of muscle-tension and pressed-phonation patients) and in voice therapy (the pressed mode contrasted with the modal mode in retraining), and maintained alongside modal, falsetto, creaky, breathy, and whisper phonation. e.g.: the pressed-voice category in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory (The Science of the Singing Voice); the pressed-voice label in a laryngology report for a patient with muscle-tension dysphonia; the pressed-voice contrast in a voice-therapy plan retraining a hyperfunctional singer | not: breathy voice (incomplete closure, reduced contact, turbulent leakage at low pressure); creaky voice (low-f0 aperiodic implosive vibration at low pressure); modal phonation (balanced contact and pressure at modal frequency) [formal: vox compressa | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Spectral-band-smoothness is a spectral analysis measure that quantifies how smoothly the per-bin energy values change across frequency within a defined frequency sub-band of a spectrum. It computes a weighted mean absolute derivative of adjacent bin energies, normalized by the sub-band's mean energy and the number of bins, yielding a dimensionless index of spectral continuity. Parameters: the frequency sub-band bounds (f_min, f_max), the FFT bin energy vector, and optionally a window function for the energy estimation. The persistence mechanism is the algorithmic computation over the sub-band's energy profile. [formal: smoothness | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.30]

The cricothyroid muscle is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired muscle forming the anterolateral wall of the larynx between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, whose contraction tilts the thyroid cartilage forward relative to the cricoid, thereby tensing and elongating the vocal folds to raise pitch. Parameters: (1) the origins — anteriorly the cricothyroid ligament and the anterior arch of the cricoid cartilage; (2) the insertion — the inferior margin and inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage; (3) the action — tilts the thyroid cartilage downward and forward on the cricoid articular facets, increasing the distance between the thyroid cartilage and vocal processes, which stretches and tenses the vocal folds; (4) the innervation — exclusively by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, making it uniquely susceptible to isolated denervation injury; (5) the functional role — the primary pitch-raising muscle, activated in high-frequency phonation, emotional vocalizations, and protective airway closure. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts and laryngology, providing the structural referent for cricothyroidotomy airway procedures and cricoarytenoidectomy surgery. e.g.: the cricothyroid muscle dissection shown in Gray's Anatomy 51st edition; the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve stimulation during thyroidectomy; cricothyroidotomy (emergency surgical airway through the cricothyroid membrane) per ATLS guidelines | not: the thyroarytenoid muscle (runs within the vocal fold and relaxes it, innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve); the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle (the only vocal fold abductor, innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve) [formal: musculus cricothyroideus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Laryngeal palpation is a manual examination technique in which the clinician uses external finger pressure on the neck to assess the position, symmetry, mobility, and sensitivity of the laryngeal cartilages and surrounding structures. Parameters: (1) the palpation regions - thyrohyoid membrane, thyroid cartilage notch, cricothyroid space, cricoid cartilage, and the lateral soft tissues of the anterior neck; (2) the assessment targets - thyroid cartilage tilt and rotation, cricothyroid joint mobility, thyrohyoid distance change during phonation, subcutaneous emphysema, and tenderness or crepitus; (3) the clinical indications - suspected laryngeal trauma, recurrent laryngeal nerve injury, laryngeal fracture, tracheoesophageal speech assessment, or preoperative airway evaluation. It persists as a maintained clinical skill in laryngology and otolaryngology training, documented in physical examination textbooks and clinical practice guidelines. e.g.: palpating the thyrohyoid membrane for increased tension during vowel phonation; assessing cricothyroid joint mobility by lateral finger pressure on the cricothyroid space; palpating the neck for crepitus following laryngeal trauma; subcutaneous emphysema on laryngeal palpation after laryngeal surgery [formal: palpatio laryngea | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The maximum flow derivative (MFD) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the peak rate of change of glottal flow within a glottal cycle, reported per cycle and aggregated over voiced frames. Given the glottal flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, MFD is computed as the maximum magnitude of the first derivative (or first difference) of g within each pitch-synchronous cycle, max |g(n+1) - g(n)|, then aggregated across cycles by the median or mean over the analyzed frames. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the derivative operator — first difference or finite difference over the sampled flow, (4) the normalization choice — absolute units (volume per sample interval) or relative to the cycle's maximum flow, and (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean). A high MFD marks a sharp glottal closure (pressed, spiky phonation) and a low MFD marks a gradual closure (breathy phonation), with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside jitter, shimmer, and the phase quotients. [formal: derivatio fluminis maxima | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

For a frequency band with N energy bins having energies E_1, E_2, ..., E_N: the RMS energy is the square root of the mean of squared energies. The parameter is the frequency band definition (lower and upper bounds). The persistence mechanism is RMS = sqrt((1/N) * sum(E_i^2)) over N bins within the band. Display trailer: [formal: rms energy | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The epiglottic cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the leaf-shaped elastic cartilage situated at the superior entrance of the larynx, whose role in covering the glottis during swallowing protects the airway from aspiration. Parameters: (1) the lamina — a thin flat plate of elastic cartilage approximately 4 cm long, with a free upper border and a narrowed stem attached to the thyroid cartilage angle; (2) the surface anatomy — the lingual surface (anterior, facing the root of the tongue) and the laryngeal surface (posterior, facing the laryngeal inlet); (3) the attachment — the epiglottic stalk attached to the posterior surface of the thyroid cartilage at an angle of approximately 40 degrees in adults. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, emergency airway management protocols, and laryngology atlases. e.g.: the epiglottic cartilage described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; the epiglottis visible on direct laryngoscopy as a landmark for endotracheal intubation; the epiglottic shape on lateral neck radiograph in a child | not: the epiglottis (the entire anatomical structure including mucosa, not just the cartilage construct); the aryepiglottic fold (mucosal fold with elastic cartilage, a distinct structure) [formal: cartilago epiglottica | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The thyroarytenoid muscle is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the paired intrinsic laryngeal muscle extending from the thyroid cartilage anteriorly to the arytenoid cartilage posteriorly, whose contraction shortens and relaxes the vocal folds to lower pitch. Parameters: (1) the origin — the inner surface of the thyroid cartilage at the angle, just below the thyroid notch; (2) the insertion — the anterior surface and lateral margin of the arytenoid cartilage, with fibers interweaving with the vocalis muscle; (3) the vocalis muscle — the deep medial fibers of the thyroarytenoid that run parallel to the vocal fold ligament, fine-tuning vocal fold tension independently of gross arytenoid rotation; (4) the action — shortens the distance between the thyroid cartilage and arytenoid, relaxing the vocal folds and decreasing tension; (5) the functional role — the primary voice relaxer, active in low-pitch phonation, and the structural substrate within which the vocal fold ligament lies. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts and laryngology, providing the structural referent for vocal fold medialization procedures and intramuscular botulinum toxin injections. e.g.: the thyroarytenoid muscle cross-section shown in Gray's Anatomy 51st edition; vocal fold medialization injection laryngoplasty targeting the vocalis muscle; intramuscular botulinum toxin injection for adductor spasmodic dysphonia at the thyroarytenoid per Benninger's protocol | not: the cricothyroid muscle (tenses vocal fold, opposite action, innervated by superior laryngeal nerve); the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle (abducts the fold, not within the fold wall) [formal: musculus thyroarytenoideus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The subglottal pressure (SGP) is a laryngeal voice-quality parameter quantifying the air pressure in the subglottal space (the trachea immediately below the vocal folds) during phonation. It is measured with a pressure transducer - typically a catheter placed through the nose or mouth, or an esophageal or transoral catheter - positioned below the glottis, and reported as the steady-state or cycle-averaged pressure during phonation, in units of cmH2O or kPa. A high SGP indicates increased laryngeal adduction effort (hyperfunctional phonation, spasmodic dysphonia, laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia); a low SGP indicates glottal insufficiency (incomplete closure, breathy phonation). Parameters: (1) the analyzed phonation segment, (2) the transducer position below the glottis (nasotracheal, transoral, or esophageal catheter), (3) the pressure reference and averaging window. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical parameter measured by transducer catheter, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained as a member of the voice-quality measurement map. e.g.: subglottal pressure from an esophageal catheter transducer in a laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia study; subglottal pressure from a nasotracheal catheter in a spasmodic-dysphonia protocol | not: glottal flow waveform; sound-pressure-level [formal: pressio subglottalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

For a spectral decomposition with N frequency bins indexed i=1..N, each with center frequency f_i and complex amplitude A_i, the per-bin energy vector is the ordered tuple v = (|A_1|², |A_2|², …, |A_N|²) of non-negative scalars ordered by bin index, each entry being the energy of its bin. It is parameterized by the decomposition and a bin range [i_min, i_max] within 1..N: at the full range the vector covers all bins of the spectrum; at a range covering exactly the bins whose centers fall in a frequency band [f_low, f_high) it is the band-restricted vector. Persistence mechanism: explicit storage of the ordered tuple as the substrate operand that spectral descriptors read their per-bin energies, means, centroids, and maxima from directly, rather than from any scalar summary. [formal: vector energiae binarum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-onset detects the emergence of new frequency content by measuring the increase in spectral energy between consecutive time frames. Given consecutive power spectra P[k,t] and P[k,t-1], the spectral onset function O[t] = max(P[k,t] - P[k,t-1], 0) summed across frequency bins. Parameters: (1) the power spectrum P[k,t] as the input domain, (2) the frame rate and windowing scheme, (3) the frequency band of interest. The persistence mechanism is the frame-to-frame difference of the power spectrum, thresholded by a half-wave rectifier, which distinguishes onset frames from sustained or decaying content. [formal: spectralis initium | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-subband partitions the frequency axis into a contiguous range [f_lower, f_upper] within the overall spectrum. Given a sampling rate F_s and N frequency bins indexed by k = 0..N-1, a subband is defined by index range [k_1, k_2] where f_lower = k_1·F_s/N and f_upper = (k_2+1)·F_s/N. Parameters: (1) the spectral resolution (bin width F_s/N), (2) the frequency range [f_lower, f_upper] defining the subband, (3) the spectral representation (power spectrum, magnitude spectrum, or coefficients) over which the subband operates. The persistence mechanism is the contiguous index range [k_1, k_2] over the frequency axis, which enables independent processing of frequency content within the band. [formal: spectralis subbanda | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The glottal source spectrum is the per-frame power spectrum of the glottal flow waveform g(n) (the glottogram): the spectral representation of the estimated glottal source over each voiced frame. Given the frame-aligned glottal-flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source - the glottal source spectrum for a frame is the power spectrum of g over that frame, typically the squared magnitude of the frame's discrete Fourier transform |G(f)|^2 (or its Welch/averaged estimate), expressed in dB and reported across the source-relevant band (classically 100-4000 Hz). Its parameters are: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, the sole operand, (2) the per-frame spectral estimate (window, overlap, averaging method), and (3) the reporting band and units (dB, the source-relevant frequency range). The source spectrum is a maintained diagnostic representation in its own right: its overall shape - the balance of energy between low and high frequencies - characterizes the glottal source and is read clinically (a steeply falling source spectrum marks a breathy, energy-decaying source; a flatter or high-frequency-forward source spectrum a bright, pressed source), and it is the operand from which the source-domain voice-quality measures (the glottal source spectral tilt, the source harmonicity, the glottal-to-noise ratio) are computed. It is reported in standardized units and persists as a maintained source-domain representation in voice-analysis toolkits and laryngology, implemented alongside the glottogram and the source parameters. [formal: spectrum fontis glottis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

The glottal pulse is the periodic excitation of airflow generated by vocal fold vibration during voiced phonation. It is the source excitation that, when filtered by the vocal-tract transfer function, produces the speech signal. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, the glottal pulse is identified per pitch period as the airflow excursion whose onset coincides with the glottal opening and whose decay returns the flow to baseline. Parameters: (1) the vocal fold vibration cycle generating the airflow pulse, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the pulse shape parameters — rise time, duration, and amplitude of the airflow excursion. It persists as a standardized source-excitation construct in speech science, implemented in voice-analysis and synthesis toolkits, taught in speech production curricula, and used to model the glottal source in source-filter separation. [formal: pulsus glottidis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Speech-language pathology is the clinical discipline of communication and swallowing: the assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of disorders of speech sounds, voice, language, fluency, cognition-communication, and swallowing, by examination and therapeutic intervention. Parameters: (1) the disorder territories - speech sound disorders, voice disorders, language disorders, fluency disorders, cognitive-communication disorders, and dysphagia; (2) the examination methods - standardized tests, perceptual evaluation, and instrumental assessment of articulation, prosody, and swallowing, with laryngeal structure referred to laryngology; (3) the treatment methods - articulation and resonance retraining, voice therapy, language therapy, fluency shaping, and swallowing therapy, each a structured protocol of goal, practice, and re-assessment; (4) the practitioner role - a licensed speech-language pathologist, certified through graduate training. It persists as a maintained discipline: licensed and certified through professional bodies, practiced in hospitals, schools, and private clinics, documented in its journals, and revised as evidence accumulates. e.g.: the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association's scope of practice and certification standards; a speech-language pathologist delivering resonant voice therapy for muscle-tension dysphonia; a speech-language pathologist providing swallowing therapy for a post-stroke dysphagia patient | not: laryngology (which examines and treats the larynx by direct visualization and surgery, not by communicative retraining) [formal: pathologia sermonis et deglutionis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Speaking fundamental frequency is a human-made acoustic parameter of speech: the average fundamental frequency of the voice signal during connected speech, measured as the mean of the fundamental frequency values across a sample of continuous speech. It is computed from a recorded speech sample by extracting the fundamental frequency at each analysis frame and averaging the values. It persists as a standardized speech parameter because it is defined by a repeatable measurement procedure applied to a recorded speech sample. e.g.: the speaking fundamental frequency measured in a patient during a voice assessment; the speaking fundamental frequency used as a baseline in a voice disorder diagnostic report; the speaking fundamental frequency compared before and after voice therapy | not: jitter (cycle-to-cycle variation of the fundamental frequency, not its mean); pitch (the perceptual attribute of fundamental frequency, not the measured parameter itself) [formal: f0 | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The glottal closure instant (GCI) is a voice-quality parameter locating the point of glottal closure within each glottal cycle: the instant at which the glottal airflow returns to baseline and the closed phase begins. In the pinned sense it is estimated from the glottal flow waveform (glottogram) g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking: within each pitch-synchronous cycle, the GCI is the time point of the cycle's minimum glottal flow - the flow trough returning to baseline - equivalently the point where the first derivative of the flow crosses zero from negative to positive. It is reported per cycle as a time point and as the normalized GCI (nGCI), the difference between successive closure instants divided by the intervening fundamental period, a dimensionless ratio with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation: a prolonged nGCI marks increased glottal closure as in spastic or hyperfunctional dysphonia, a shortened nGCI a breathy, insufficiently closed source. Parameters: (1) the glottal flow waveform g(n) - the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the per-cycle window, (3) the closure operator - the flow-minimum location, the first-derivative zero crossing from negative to positive within the cycle, (4) the normalized reporting - nGCI as a dimensionless ratio, (5) the cross-cycle aggregation (median or mean over the analyzed frames). It is reported in standardized units and persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits, documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology, and maintained alongside the closure quotient, the open quotient, the maximum flow derivative, and the return phase. [formal: instant clausurae glottidis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Voice range profile is a human-made graph that maps a speaker's voice across pitch and loudness: the range of fundamental frequencies a voice can produce at each loudness level, plotted as a region in the frequency-intensity plane. It is generated by recording a voice while the speaker phonates sustained vowels across a pitch and loudness sweep, measuring the fundamental frequency and sound pressure level at each point, and plotting the outermost boundary of the achievable region. It persists as a standardized clinical tool because it is defined by a repeatable recording and plotting procedure applied to a voice sample. e.g.: a voice range profile plotted for a patient with vocal fold paralysis during a voice assessment; a normative voice range profile used as a reference in a voice clinic; a voice range profile compared before and after voice therapy to track recovery | not: spectrogram (a time-frequency visual display of a voice signal, not a pitch-loudness boundary map); audiogram (a hearing threshold plot across frequency, not a voice production map) [formal: vocogram | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Text-linguistics is a human-made discipline of linguistics — the study of the structure, coherence, and function of extended texts (discourses) as structured wholes that extend beyond the sentence level. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the unit of analysis is the text or discourse as an integrated semantic-pragmatic entity, governed by relations of cohesion (grammatical and lexical ties across clauses), coherence (understandable logical and semantic connections), and communicative purpose (the function the text serves in interaction); (2) the analytical tools include discourse structure analysis (narrative, argumentative, expository patterns), information structure (theme-rheme, given-new), referential continuity (pronoun chains, anaphora resolution), and textual genre conventions that organize texts for specific communicative situations. Text-linguistics persists as a discipline that produces descriptions of textual organization across languages, models of discourse interpretation, and applications in text technology, rhetoric, discourse analysis, and language pedagogy. Paradigmatic cases: Halliday and Hasan's cohesion analysis, van Dijk's discourse semantics, rhetorical structure theory. [formal: textus-linguistica | substrate: mind | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Spectral-median (median frequency) is the full-spectrum energy-quantile summary that reports the frequency f_med at which half of the total spectral energy lies below and half above. Parameters: (1) the per-bin energy vector E = {E_i} over the full analyzed spectrum [f0, f_max), (2) the energy-weighted cumulative distribution C(f) = (sum of E_i for bins at frequency <= f) / (sum of all E_i), (3) the target quantile q, which the median fixes at q = 0.5; the reported value is the smallest frequency f such that C(f) >= q. It is a member of the same quantile family as spectral-rolloff, which fixes q at the 85% energy level: the median is the 50% level of that family and does not depend on a chosen high-level contour. It reads the full per-bin energy vector and carries no [f_low, f_high) band bounds, so it is a full-side summary rather than a band-local one. Persists as a standard energy-quantile summary in audio analysis, computed on the per-bin energy vector in MIR toolkits and reported in sound-description documentation. [formal: mediana spectri | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-crossover is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the median energy location of a full spectrum at a given analysis frame, unbounded by any sub-band: the frequency at which the cumulative energy reaches 50 percent of the spectrum's total energy. Parameters: (1) the full set of frequency bins i=1..N with center frequencies f_i, (2) the per-bin energy values E_i = |A_i|^2 over the whole spectrum, (3) the analysis frame window. Computed by ordering the bins in ascending frequency, accumulating the per-bin energies until the running total first reaches half of the total energy sum, and taking the center frequency of the bin at that crossing. The value is in hertz: a low crossover means most energy sits below the median frequency (dark spectrum), a high crossover means energy is pushed toward the upper bins (bright spectrum). It is the whole-spectrum counterpart of spectral-band-crossover, which restricts the same cumulative test to bins within [f_low, f_high). It differs from spectral-centroid (energy-weighted mean, sensitive to high-energy outliers) and from spectral-rolloff (the cumulative crossing at an arbitrary threshold such as 85 percent, measuring brightness rather than the median). Being the 50th percentile of the energy distribution, the crossover is robust to heavy-tailed energy. Persistence: the standardized mathematical definition of the full-spectrum energy median in spectral analysis, implemented in audio analysis toolkits and MIR feature pipelines. [formal: medium spectrale | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Videolaryngoscopy is laryngoscopy performed with the laryngeal image displayed on a video monitor: a camera at the tip of the scope replaces the direct line of sight, so the image is recorded, transmitted, and shared while the instrument is in place. Its parameters are the camera-integrated scope (a flexible fiberoptic with a video camera for the voice-medicine route, a camera-tipped blade for the airway route), the display, and the laryngeal field; it persists as a maintained standard in ENT, anesthesiology, and voice-medicine references, with a defined instrument set and a display field. e.g.: flexible video laryngoscopy for voice evaluation; intubation with a GlideScope camera blade | not: direct laryngoscopy with a mirror [formal: videolaryngoscopia | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Spectral-concentration is a spectral analysis measure quantifying how much of a spectrum's total energy is concentrated in a single specified bin, normalized by the spectrum's total energy. Given a spectrum with N bins having energies E_1, E_2, ..., E_N, the concentration at bin j is C_j = E_j / Σ_i E_i. The value ranges from 0 (energy spread across all bins) to approaching 1 (nearly all energy in one bin). Parameters: (1) the spectral estimate (periodogram, Welch's method, or spectrogram slice), (2) the per-bin energy vector across all frequency bins, (3) the target bin index j. Persistence mechanism: standardized definition of normalized per-bin energy share, used in audio analysis, speech processing, and music information retrieval as a level-invariant spectral descriptor. [formal: concentratio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Pressed voice (pressed phonation, hyperfunctional phonation) is a classification category for a mode of voiced phonation defined by a specific glottal configuration: the vocal folds are pressed together with excessive medial compression, so that each cycle carries a prolonged closed phase and an abrupt, steep opening. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal configuration - excessive medial compression of the folds with prolonged complete closure during each vibration cycle, (2) the cycle signature - a shortened open phase and a lengthened closed phase relative to the fundamental period (a high contact quotient, a low open quotient), a short rise time, and a steep flow declination, (3) the acoustic signature - a harsh, strained, or pressed timbre with reduced harmonic-to-noise contrast and reduced glottal airflow. It persists as a named mode of the phonation-mode taxonomy: documented in laryngology (spastic and hyperfunctional dysphonia, muscle-tension dysphonia), used in voice-disorder assessment and voice therapy, and maintained alongside modal, breathy, falsetto, creaky, and whisper phonation. e.g.: the pressed (hyperfunctional) category in a voice-disorder assessment of muscle-tension dysphonia; the pressed-voice label in a laryngoscopy report of spastic dysphonia; the pressed category in Sundberg's five-mode phonation inventory | not: creaky voice (low-frequency implosive vibration, a different mode); breathy voice (incomplete closure with noise leak, a different mode); modal phonation (complete closure at modal timing, a different mode) [formal: vox compressa | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Closure quotient (CQ) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the fraction of the fundamental period during which the glottis is closed in voiced phonation. From the frame-aligned glottal-flow waveform g(n) (glottogram) and the fundamental period T0, the closed phase is the interval between the flow minimum (Fmin) and the next flow maximum (Fmax) - or between the zero crossings of the flow derivative bounding the closed phase - and CQ = closed phase / T0, so CQ = 1 - OQ for the same frame. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the closed-phase extraction method (Fmin-Fmax difference or flow-derivative zero crossings). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; the maintained reference range for typical phonation sits near 0.3-0.5, and an elevated closure quotient indicates prolonged glottal closure as in breathy or dysphonic phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software (Praat, laryngology suites) from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: quota clausurae | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Vocal-fold-closure-efficiency is a quantitative metric that expresses the proportion of glottal closure achieved during phonation, derived from aerodynamic or imaging measures of airflow and contact area. Parameters: (1) measurement modality - aerodynamic flow, electroglottography contact quotient, or high-speed video contact area; (2) normalization - ratio of measured closure to maximal achievable closure under the same subglottal pressure; (3) reporting units - percentage or dimensionless ratio. It persists as a maintained analytic construct in voice research and clinical voice assessment, documented in peer-reviewed methods and software toolkits. e.g.: 85% closure efficiency measured by electroglottography in normal phonation; 40% efficiency in unilateral vocal fold paralysis measured by aerodynamic flow; high-speed video showing 92% contact area in trained singers | not: vocal fold mobility, which assesses movement rather than closure completeness; fundamental frequency, which measures pitch rather than closure [formal: efficientia clausurae plicae vocalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

Residual signal is the per-sample difference signal r(n) = x(n) - x_hat(n), where x(n) is the observed signal and x_hat(n) is the reconstructed signal produced by a model system. The residual-signal captures what the model fails to account for: in speech processing, it is the glottal excitation waveform after removing the vocal-tract filter; in system identification, it is the model-error waveform that reveals unmodeled dynamics or noise. Computed by: (1) obtaining the model (e.g., an all-pole linear-prediction filter), (2) filtering the input to produce the model output, (3) subtracting the model output from the observed signal. Parameters: (1) the observed signal x(n), (2) the model structure and parameters, (3) the subtraction method. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation in DSP software (Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documentation in signal processing literature, and standardized use in model evaluation, speech analysis, and adaptive filtering. [formal: residualis-signalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The vocal-tract model is a human-made model of the vocal tract as an acoustic filter cavity in speech production, describing how the shape of the vocal tract resonates to shape the glottal source into speech sounds. Parameters: area function along tract length, formant frequencies and bandwidths, articulatory positions. Persistence mechanism: the model is formalized as acoustic tube theory, implemented in speech synthesis and analysis software, and taught in phonetics; it persists as a reusable filter component of the source-filter framework. [formal: vocal-tract | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.07]

Vocal fold vibration is a human-authored biomechanical construct that models the periodic, self-sustained oscillation of the paired vocal folds driven by the interaction of subglottal aerodynamic pressure and tissue elasticity — the myoelastic-aerodynamic mechanism that converts steady airflow into periodic acoustic excitation. Parameters: (1) the driving forces — subglottal pressure buildup, Bernoulli suction during glottal convergence, and tissue elastic restoring force; (2) the tissue properties — the layered viscoelasticity of the lamina propria (governed by the stiffness gradient from superficial to deep layers), the mass of the mucosal cover, and the tension set by the thyroarytenoid and cricothyroid muscles; (3) the oscillatory regime — the fundamental frequency (f0) determined by the balance of aerodynamic driving force and tissue stiffness, the amplitude of vibration reflecting the degree of abduction, and the mucosal wave traveling from inferior to superior fold surface. It persists in voice research as a standard biomechanical model, in clinical assessment via stroboscopy and high-speed videolaryngoscopy, and in speech synthesis as the source excitation model. e.g.: the mucosal wave model described in Hirano's structural model of phonation; the two-mass model of vocal fold vibration by Ishizaka and Flanagan, 1972 | not: the glottal flow waveform, which is the acoustic output of vibration rather than the mechanical motion itself [formal: vibratio plicarum vocalium | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

Glottal flow derivative is the first time derivative of the glottal flow waveform g(t), quantifying the instantaneous rate of change of glottal airflow. Computed numerically from the sampled glottal-flow estimate g(n) as the first difference g(n+1) - g(n), optionally normalized by the sampling interval to yield units of volume per second. The positive branch (derivative > 0) corresponds to the opening phase of the glottal cycle; the negative branch (derivative < 0) corresponds to the closing phase. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the sampling interval Δt from the signal's sampling rate, (3) the numerical differentiation method (forward, backward, or central difference). Persistence mechanism: the standardized signal-processing construct implemented in voice-analysis software, documented in the Klatt and Klatt glottal-source parameter set, and maintained as the foundational derivative measure from which glottal-flow-declination-rate and maximum-flow-derivative are derived. e.g.: glottal-flow derivative used as the input to glottal-flow-declination-rate computation in the Dewaele parameter set; glottal-flow derivative waveform displayed in a Praat glottogram analysis panel; glottal-flow derivative computed from an EGG-based glottogram in a voice-disorder assessment of vocal fold paralysis | not: glottal-flow-declination-rate (a derived scalar, not the full derivative function); maximum-flow-derivative (a derived scalar, not the full derivative function) [formal: derivata fluminis glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

The attack-time is a non-negative real-valued duration representing the time elapsed from the onset of a sound to the peak of its amplitude envelope. Parameters: (1) the amplitude envelope function of the sound, (2) the detected onset point (zero-crossing of the envelope derivative), (3) the peak point (global maximum of the envelope within the attack phase). The persistence mechanism identifies the onset as the first zero-crossing of the envelope's first derivative after silence, and the peak as the local maximum of the envelope following that onset, then computes the time difference. [formal: attack-time | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

Spectral increase is a metric capturing the temporal rise of spectral energy between consecutive analysis frames. Computed as the difference between the current frame's total spectral energy and the preceding frame's energy, normalized by the preceding frame's energy. Positive values indicate energy growth; negative values indicate decay. [formal: augmentatio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A patient-reported outcome measure in which individuals rate their own voice disorder's impact on daily functioning across functional, physical, and emotional domains using a validated 30-item Likert-scale questionnaire. The construct persists as a standardized instrument maintained by the Voice Handicap Index developers and adopted by ASHA clinical guidelines, scoring protocols, and voice-disorder outcome research. e.g.: the Voice Handicap Index (VHI-30) administered to patients with vocal nodules at pre- and post-surgical follow-up; the VHI-10 screening form used in laryngology triage; the Voice Handicap Index-Effect subscale score reported in a voice-surgery quality-of-life study | not: GRBAS, which is a clinician-rated perceptual scale, not a patient self-report; CAPE-V, which is a trained rater's perceptual severity assessment, not a patient questionnaire [formal: index impedimenti vocis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

Asymmetry coefficient is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the asymmetry of the glottal airflow pulse within each glottal cycle: the ratio of the rising phase duration to the falling phase duration of the first derivative of the glottal flow waveform. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, the glottal cycle is partitioned into the rising phase (where g'(n) is positive, from minimum to maximum) and the falling phase (where g'(n) is negative, from maximum to minimum); the asymmetry coefficient is rising-phase duration / falling-phase duration. A coefficient near 1 indicates a symmetric pulse (typical modal phonation), while deviation from 1 indicates asymmetric closure — a longer falling phase (coefficient < 1) marks abrupt closure in pressed phonation, and a longer rising phase (coefficient > 1) indicates gradual closure in breathy phonation. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform g(n) — the inverse-filtering estimate of the glottal source, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking which frames the cycle, (3) the first derivative of g(n) to locate phase boundaries. It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; maintained reference ranges separate typical from disordered phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed from the glottogram by voice-analysis software (Praat, laryngology suites), documented in the Dewaele glottal-source parameter set, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and maintained alongside the maximum-flow-derivative, the glottal-flow-declination-rate, the phase quotients, and the other glottal source parameters as a member of the voice-quality measurement map. e.g.: the asymmetry coefficient reported in a laryngology study comparing pressed and breathy phonation types; the asymmetry coefficient computed from a glottal-flow waveform in a laryngeal dysphonia case; the asymmetry coefficient value of 0.85 measured in a pressed-phonation assessment | not: glottal-flow-declination-rate (the steepest negative slope, not a ratio); maximum-flow-derivative (the peak positive slope, not a ratio) [formal: coeficiens inaequalitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

spectral-band-peak(f_low, f_high) = max{E[i]} for all bins i where f_low <= f_center[i] < f_high. Parameters: f_low (Hz, lower band boundary), f_high (Hz, upper band boundary), sampling_rate (Hz, determines bin center frequencies), n_fft (int, FFT window size). Persistence: pointwise maximum of the power spectral density within the band. [formal: spectral-band-peak | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The energy-envelope is the per-frame time series of a signal's energy, a human-made representation derived from a discrete-time waveform by framing, windowing, and magnitude squaring. Parameters: (1) the analysis frame length (typically 20-40 ms), (2) the hop between successive frames, (3) the window function applied within each frame (e.g. Hamming, Hanning), and (4) the squaring convention - raw x^2(t), windowed |w(t) x(t)|^2, or the per-frame sum that projects to short-time-energy as its scalar value. Distinction: it is the energy series, not the per-frame scalar (short-time-energy) and not the per-sample Hilbert amplitude (amplitude-envelope); it is the operand on which temporal-centroid (first moment of the energy envelope) and onset-related energy readings operate. Persistence mechanism: standardized windowed computation across audio analysis and speech toolkits (librosa, Essentia, HTK, Praat), encoded in published feature-extraction pipelines. [formal: envelopium energiae | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The spectral-power-distribution is a non-negative real-valued function over a discrete frequency domain representing how signal power is distributed across frequency bins. Parameters: (1) the input signal, (2) the number of frequency bins N, (3) the sampling rate or frequency resolution. Computation: take the magnitude spectrum |X[k]| of the input signal, compute P[k] = |X[k]|² / N for each bin k, yielding a discrete distribution over frequencies. The values P[k] are non-negative and sum to the total signal power, forming a power distribution across the frequency axis. [formal: CONCEPT | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-band-variance is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the dispersion of spectral energy within a defined frequency sub-band of a spectrum at a given analysis frame. It is the band-localized (second-moment) statistic of the spectral-band moment family, computed from the per-bin energy values inside the band. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds (f_low, f_high, e.g. ISO 266 third-octave band edges or analyst-specified limits), (2) the per-bin energy array E_i = |X[k]|^2 indexed by the frequency bins whose centers fall within [f_low, f_high). Computation: the within-band mean mu = (1/N) SUM E_i, then the within-band variance sigma^2 = (1/N) SUM (E_i - mu)^2; the result is a single scalar per frame, typically in normalized relative units or joules squared. It measures how spread out the energy is across the band's bins: a concentrated band (one dominant bin) has low band-variance, an evenly spread band has high. Persistence: recomputed from the input spectrum and the band boundaries at any point in an audio analysis pipeline; it is the second-moment counterpart of spectral-band-centroid (first moment) and the even-order companion to spectral-band-skewness (third) and spectral-band-kurtosis (fourth). Display: {variance, low_hz, high_hz, bins, mean_energy}. [formal: varietas spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Vocal-fold-granuloma is the human-authored anatomical-diagnostic construct identifying the inflammatory reactive granulation tissue that forms on the vocal fold mucosa in response to trauma or irritation. Parameters: (1) the etiology - intubation trauma (most common), laryngopharyngeal reflux, or surgical injury, with intubation-related lesions typically arising at the posterior third of the vocal fold near the vocal process; (2) the morphology - erythematous, pedunculated or sessile mass of granulation tissue projecting from the vocal fold surface, often with a fibrous base and neovascularization; (3) the clinical presentation - hoarseness, throat pain, globus sensation, chronic cough, and vocal effort, with symptoms often worsened by reflux; (4) the differential from neoplasia - granulation tissue lacks the architectural atypia of malignancy on histology, but may mimic carcinoma clinically requiring biopsy when atypical. It persists as a maintained diagnostic category in laryngology practice: documented in laryngology textbooks and clinical case series, classified under J38.5 (other disorders of vocal cords), managed through reflux treatment, voice therapy, and when refractory, surgical excision or botulinum toxin injection. e.g.: endoscopic image of posterior glottic granuloma adjacent to the vocal process; The Laryngoscope clinical case report of intubation-related vocal fold granuloma; Rosen's Phonomicrosurgery textbook management algorithm for refractory granulomas | not: laryngeal papilloma (HPV-related epithelial neoplasm with different histology); squamous cell carcinoma of the vocal fold (malignant neoplasm with cellular atypia) [formal: granuloma cordis vocalis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

[formal: envelopeum inceptionis | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Jitter RAP (relative average perturbation) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the relative average of second-order cycle-to-cycle period differences, computed as the mean absolute value of the second difference of consecutive pitch periods divided by the mean pitch period, expressed in percent. For N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, RAP equals the sum over i from 2 to N-1 of the absolute value of P_{i+1} minus 2 times P_i plus P_{i-1}, divided by N minus 2, all divided by the mean of all P_i. Parameters: the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, and the per-cycle fundamental period from pitch tracking. Small RAP indicates smooth, stable period progression (normal phonation); large RAP indicates erratic period changes (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software from pitch-synchronous period tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment and clinical voice analysis reports. e.g.: The RAP jitter value displayed in the Kay Bolt MDVP jitter analysis report panel; RAP computed from sustained vowel phonation in the GRBAS voice assessment protocol using MDVP software; RAP reported in the acoustic analysis of dysphonia severity in the laryngology literature by Dewaele et al. | not: APQ1 using first-order average absolute difference; JRR the jitter ratio using simple cycle-to-cycle difference; shimmer using amplitude perturbation rather than period perturbation [formal: titubatio relativa | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

Spectral-band-evenness is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying how uniformly energy is distributed across the frequency bins within a defined frequency sub-band, normalized by the band's mean energy. It is the coefficient of variation of the per-bin energy values: given a band with N bins having energies E_i for i=1..N, the evenness is σ/μ where μ = (1/N)·ΣE_i is the mean energy and σ = √((1/N)·Σ(E_i - μ)²) is the standard deviation of energies. The value is a dimensionless ratio: 0 when all bins carry identical energy (perfectly even), increasing without upper bound as energy becomes more concentrated in fewer bins. Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds (f_low, f_high), (2) the per-bin energy vector E_i within those bounds. Persistence mechanism: standardized definition of energy dispersion normalized by mean, used in music information retrieval and audio classification as a level-invariant spectral descriptor. [formal: aequabilitas spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Formant frequency is a human-made acoustic parameter of speech: a resonance frequency of the vocal tract that appears as a concentration of energy in the speech spectrum. It is measured from a recorded speech signal by identifying the peaks in the spectral envelope — the local maxima of the magnitude spectrum — and is labeled F1, F2, F3, etc. in order of increasing frequency. It persists as a standardized speech parameter because it is defined by a repeatable spectral analysis procedure applied to a recorded utterance. e.g.: the first formant frequency measured in a vowel produced by a speaker during a speech analysis; the formant frequency values used in a speech recognition system to distinguish vowel sounds; a formant frequency measured in a clinical voice assessment to evaluate vocal tract configuration | not: fundamental frequency (the vibration rate of the vocal folds, not a vocal tract resonance); harmonic (an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency, not a vocal tract resonance peak) [formal: formanta | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The interarytenoid muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the unpaired intrinsic laryngeal muscle spanning between the two arytenoid cartilages posterior to the glottis, whose contraction adducts the arytenoids and narrows the posterior glottic chink. Parameters: (1) the oblique fibers — the most important portion, extending from the muscular process of one arytenoid to the apex and lateral margin of the opposite arytenoid, crossing in a diagonal fashion; (2) the transverse fibers — a shallow layer spanning the posterior surfaces of both arytenoids without crossing; (3) the action — pulls the arytenoid cartilages toward each other, approximating their vocal processes and narrowing the posterior glottic aperture; (4) the functional role — primary adductor of the posterior glottis, working with the lateral cricoarytenoid muscles for complete vocal fold closure, and contributing to airway protection during swallowing. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology classification systems, and surgical anatomy references. e.g.: the interarytenoid muscle described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; the interarytenoid muscle identified during posterior laryngoscopy as a bulge between the arytenoids; the interarytenoid atrophy noted in unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy | not: the lateral-cricoarytenoid-muscle (adducts the vocal folds but from the cricoid to the arytenoid, a distinct muscle); the posterior-cricoarytenoid-muscle (the abductor acting on the arytenoids from the opposite direction) [formal: muscular interarytaenoideum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The reduction of spectral energy from its peak value across frequency bins. Parameters: (1) discrete power spectrum P[k] for k = 0, ..., N-1 where N is the number of frequency bins, (2) the maximum power value P_max = max_k(P[k]). Persistence mechanism: computed as D[k] = P_max - P[k] for each bin k, yielding a per-bin spectral decrease value; alternatively aggregated as a scalar S = (1/N) * Σ_k(P_max - P[k]) over all bins. Display trailer: spectral-decrease is a scalar or per-bin quantity expressed in the same units as the power spectrum. [formal: diminutio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds, (2) the spectral energy values across frequency bins within the band. Computed by sorting frequency bins in ascending order by frequency, accumulating energy until the accumulated total reaches half the band's total energy; the frequency at that point is the crossover point. Distinct from spectral-band-centroid (weighted mean, sensitive to energy outliers) and spectral-band-rolloff (arbitrary threshold like 85%, indicating brightness); the crossover is the energy-median, robust to heavy-tailed distributions. Displayed as a scalar time series over analysis frames. [formal: centrum medium spectrale | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An analytic signal is a human-made complex-valued signal representation constructed from a real-valued signal x(t) by adding its Hilbert transform H{x(t)} as the imaginary component: z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}. This construction eliminates all negative-frequency components, resulting in a one-sided spectrum. The analytic signal carries three directly accessible parameters: (1) instantaneous amplitude (envelope) A(t) = |z(t)| = √(x(t)² + H{x(t)}²), (2) instantaneous phase φ(t) = arg(z(t)), and (3) instantaneous frequency f_inst(t) = (1/2π)·dφ/dt. These parameters are computable in real time from a single observation, without ensemble averaging. The construction is used in communications (quadrature modulation/demodulation, SSB generation), audio analysis (phase vocoder phase unwrapping), geophysics, and biomedical signal processing. Persistence mechanism: algorithmic computation standard in DSP libraries (scipy.signal.hilbert, MATLAB hilbert) and embedded in communication system designs. [formal: signalis analyticus | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Glottal closure index (GCI) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the degree of vocal fold contact during voiced phonation, computed from the electroglottographic (EGG) signal. Given the EGG waveform, GCI is calculated as GCI = (EGG_max - EGG_min) / EGG_max, where EGG_max is the maximum amplitude of the EGG signal during the glottal cycle (corresponding to maximum vocal fold contact) and EGG_min is the minimum amplitude (corresponding to minimum contact). GCI ranges from 0 (no contact) to 1 (complete contact). Its parameters are: (1) the EGG waveform, (2) the identification of EGG_max and EGG_min per cycle, (3) the normalization by EGG_max. A high GCI indicates strong, complete closure (pressed phonation); a low GCI indicates incomplete closure (breathy phonation). It persists as a standardized clinical parameter computed by EGG analysis software, documented in the EGG literature (Ducasse, Mees, Sivasakthi), and used in voice disorder assessment. e.g.: GCI computed from an EGG signal in a laryngology study of muscle-tension dysphonia; the mean GCI reported for subjects with vocal fold paralysis in a clinical trial; GCI values from the EGG analysis module in Praat for sustained vowel phonation | not: contact-quotient (a temporal duration ratio, not an amplitude ratio); EGG signal (the raw measurement, not the derived index) [formal: index contactus glottidis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

Spectral-band-asymmetry is a statistical descriptor quantifying how unevenly spectral energy is distributed across the frequency bins within a defined sub-band. Parameters: (1) lower and upper frequency bounds of the sub-band, (2) the energy values per frequency bin within the band. Computed as the normalized sum of absolute deviations from the band centroid: A = sum_i(|f_i - f_c| * E_i) / sum_i(E_i), where f_i is the frequency of bin i, f_c is the band centroid (weighted mean frequency), and E_i is the energy in bin i. The value is expressed in Hertz and indicates the spatial spread of energy around the centroid — higher values mean energy is concentrated toward one edge of the band, lower values mean energy is more centrally distributed. Persistence mechanism: arithmetic computation over the finite set of per-bin energy values for the given band and analysis frame. [formal: asymmetria spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Instantaneous frequency is a human-made signal processing construct that measures the rate of change of the phase of a signal at each moment in time. It is defined as: f_inst(t) = (1/2π)·dφ(t)/dt, where φ(t) = arg(z(t)) is the instantaneous phase of the analytic signal z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}, constructed from a real-valued signal x(t) and its Hilbert transform H{x(t)}. Unlike Fourier frequency (which represents a global property of the signal), instantaneous frequency is a local, time-varying quantity that tracks frequency modulation, chirp signals, and time-varying spectral content in real time. Parameters: (1) the phase unwrapping method applied to φ(t) (to avoid discontinuities at ±π), (2) the noise regularization method (to prevent divergence where amplitude is near zero). Persistence mechanism: standard in radar (chirp signal analysis), seismology, speech processing (formant tracking), and biomedical engineering (EEG/ECG frequency modulation analysis), implemented in DSP libraries and embedded in signal analysis instruments. [formal: frequency instantanea | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-peak-trough-ratio is a human-made spectral feature quantifying the contrast between dominant spectral peaks and the valleys between them within a defined frequency range. It is computed by first identifying local maxima (peaks) and minima (troughs) in the magnitude spectrum, then calculating the ratio of mean peak energy to mean trough energy: PTR = mean(E_peak) / mean(E_trough). Parameters: (1) a frequency range or band over which to compute the ratio, (2) a minimum peak height threshold to distinguish true peaks from noise, (3) a minimum distance between adjacent peaks. Values greater than 1 indicate a spectrum with prominent peaks above the trough floor; higher values indicate sharper, more tonal spectra. Persistence mechanism: computed numerically from discrete magnitude spectra, stored as a scalar value per analysis frame. [formal: ratio culminis et vallis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The spectral-band-concentration is a CONCEPT that quantifies how much of the total spectral power is concentrated in a subset of frequency bins. Computed as the ratio P_max/P_total where P_max is the maximum single-bin power, or equivalently via the Shannon entropy H = -Σp_i·log(p_i) of the normalized distribution p_i = P_i/P_total, with concentration = exp(-H) normalized to [0,1]. Persistence: the scalar value is maintained for a given spectral band as long as the underlying spectral representation is stable. Injection laryngoplasty is a laryngeal surgical technique that restores glottic closure by injecting a viscoelastic filler medial to the vocal fold, so the paralyzed or atrophic fold is carried toward the midline during phonation. The asymmetry coefficient is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the asymmetry of the glottal airflow pulse in voiced phonation. It measures the degree to which the glottal flow pulse is skewed toward the open or close phase of the glottal cycle. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0, the asymmetry coefficient is computed as the ratio of the open-phase duration to the close-phase duration within the period, or equivalently as the skewness of the flow pulse. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the asymmetry computation method (open-phase/close-phase ratio or flow-pulse skewness). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; a value of 1 indicates symmetric phonation, while values deviating from 1 indicate pressed (value above 1) or breathy (value below 1) phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. Shimmer (amplitude perturbation) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the cycle-to-cycle variation of amplitude in a voiced speech signal. For a voiced segment segmented into N consecutive glottal cycles, each with amplitude A_i (peak or RMS of cycle i), the perturbation is the normalized cycle difference: APQ3 = (1/(3N)) * sum_i |A_{i+1} - A_i| / ( (1/N) * sum_i A_i ), or equivalently the standard deviation of the cycle amplitudes divided by their mean, reported in percent or in dB (20*log10(std/mean)). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal segmented at pitch-synchronous cycle boundaries, (2) the per-cycle amplitude measure (peak or RMS), (3) the perturbation variant (APQ3 quotient or standard deviation). Small shimmer indicates amplitude stability (normal phonation); large shimmer indicates amplitude instability (dysphonia). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by acoustic analysis software (Praat, laryngology toolkits) from pitch-synchronous amplitude tracks; it persists as a documented measurement in voice-disorder assessment. [formal: scintillatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Stroboscopy is a clinical visualization technique that uses brief, periodic flashes of light synchronized to the vocal folds' fundamental frequency to create the illusion of slow-motion or stationary vibration. Given the fundamental period T0 estimated from pitch tracking, a strobe light fires at intervals of T0 (or a subharmonic) so that each flash illuminates the vocal folds at the same phase of their vibratory cycle. Parameters: (1) the flash duration — brief pulses (typically microseconds to milliseconds) to freeze motion, (2) the synchronization interval — derived from the estimated fundamental frequency so that successive flashes sample the same vibratory phase, (3) the illumination source — xenon strobe or LED array positioned through the laryngoscope. It persists as a maintained clinical instrument: the strobe scope system (Karl Storz, Richard Wolf), the synchronization electronics, and the standardized examination protocol. e.g.: the Karl Storz laryngeal stroboscope used for voice evaluation; the Richard Wolf LED-based laryngeal stroboscopy system | not: high-speed videolaryngoscopy — real-time recording of actual vibration at thousands of frames per second [formal: strobosopia | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]
