Closed quotient is the voice-quality measure expressing the proportion of the glottal cycle during which the vocal folds remain in contact: the closed-phase duration divided by the glottal-cycle period. It is computed from the glottal-flow waveform g(t) and the glottal-cycle period T0: the closed phase runs from glottal-pulse onset to the instant the flow returns to baseline, and the quotient is the closed-phase duration divided by T0. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform g(t) frame-aligned to voicing, (2) the glottal-cycle period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the closed-phase boundary detected from the flow derivative zero-crossings. It persists as a per-frame voice-quality measure in speech analysis toolkits and clinical voice assessment, reported alongside open quotient and shimmer in voice disorder analysis. e.g.: the closed quotient measured by glottal-flow inverse filtering in Praat for a sustained vowel /a/; the closed quotient values reported in clinical studies of vocal fold nodules; the closed quotient parameter in the Liljens-Forsberg glottal source model | not: open quotient (the complementary measure: open phase divided by glottal cycle) [formal: clausura glottalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

The Hilbert transform is a linear operator that shifts the phase of every frequency component of a real-valued signal by 90 degrees (π/2 radians). Mathematically, for a signal x(t), the Hilbert transform is: H{x(t)} = (1/π) PV ∫₋∞^∞ x(τ)/(t−τ) dτ, where PV denotes the Cauchy principal value. In the frequency domain, it acts as an all-pass filter with frequency response H(f) = −j·sgn(f), multiplying positive frequencies by −j and negative frequencies by +j. The transform produces the quadrature component of x(t); combining x(t) with its Hilbert transform yields the analytic signal z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}, from which instantaneous amplitude (envelope), instantaneous phase, and instantaneous frequency can be derived. Parameters: (1) the input signal domain (continuous-time or discrete via DFT-based implementation), (2) handling of the zero-frequency component (typically set to 0). Persistence mechanism: implemented in DSP libraries (scipy.signal.hilbert, MATLAB hilbert), used in communications (SSB modulation/demodulation), geophysics, and vibration analysis. [formal: transform Hilbert | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

source-filter-separation is a human-made signal processing technique that decomposes an observed signal into two additive or convolutive components: a source (excitation) component representing the energy origin, and a filter (resonance) component representing the shaping mechanism. The technique operates by applying one of several decomposition methods — (1) inverse filtering, where the estimated transfer function H(z) is inverted to recover e(n) = x(n) * H_inv(z), (2) deconvolution, where the source is recovered by frequency-domain division of the spectrum by the filter spectrum, or (3) cepstral analysis, where the logarithm of the spectrum separates slowly-varying filter envelope from rapidly-varying source structure. Parameters: (1) the input signal x(n), (2) the source-filter model assumptions (convolutive vs additive), (3) the decomposition method and its parameters. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation in DSP software (Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documentation in signal processing textbooks (Rabiner and Schafer, Oppenheim and Schafer), and standardized use in speech analysis, audio processing, and system identification pipelines. [formal: separatio fontis-filtrum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The glottal inertia quotient (GIQ) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the shape of the glottal area cycle: the ratio of the first to the zeroth moment of the glottal area waveform A(t) within each glottal cycle, GIQ = I1 / I0, where I_k = the integral of (t/T0)^k * A(t) dt over the cycle window T0. A high GIQ marks a late, sharply peaked area cycle (creaky voice, lobe formation); a low GIQ marks an early, rounded area cycle (breathy, hyperfunctional phonation), with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. Its parameters are: (1) the glottal area waveform A(t) per voiced frame - estimated from the electroglottographic signal derivative or from the glottal-flow waveform through a glottal-area model, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, which frames the cycle window and normalizes the moment integrals, (3) the moment order (first over zeroth). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio and persists as a member of the glottal-source parameter set in voice-disorder assessment: implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Kay Elite, laryngology suites), documented in laryngology and speech-language pathology (the Dewaele glottal-source parameter set), and maintained alongside the maximum flow derivative, the glottal closure instant, and the phase quotients. e.g.: GIQ computed from an EGG-derived glottal area waveform in a creaky-voice case report; GIQ reported in a laryngology study of muscle-tension dysphonia; GIQ of a sustained /a/ vowel in a voice-disorder cohort analysis | not: contact quotient (a phase-duration fraction of T0, not a moment of the area cycle); glottal closure instant (a time point, not a shape ratio) [formal: quota inertiae glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

The source harmonicity is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the balance between the periodic (harmonic) and the aperiodic (noise-like) components of the glottal source. It is computed from the glottal source spectrum - the per-frame power spectrum of the glottal-flow waveform g(n) (the glottogram) - which is the sole operand: the harmonic energy is measured over the frequency bands at the fundamental f0 and its integer harmonics, the aperiodic energy over the inter-harmonic regions, and the ratio is formed over the source-relevant band. Parameters: (1) the glottal source spectrum - the per-frame power spectrum of g(n), the sole operand, (2) the fundamental-frequency estimate f0 locating the harmonic comb, (3) the number of harmonics covered and the band widths around each harmonic, and (4) the ratio form of the measure, E_harmonic / (E_harmonic + E_aperiodic), a value in [0, 1]. A high value marks a dominantly periodic (modal) source and a low value an aperiodic (breathy, harsh, or dysphonic) source; it is reported as a dimensionless ratio with maintained reference ranges separating typical from disordered phonation. Spectral-band-kurtosis is a spectral analysis parameter measuring the fourth standardized moment of spectral energy distribution within a defined frequency sub-band. Computed as E[(E - μ)⁴] / σ⁴ where E is spectral energy, μ is the band-mean energy, and σ is the band-standard deviation. High kurtosis indicates a distribution with heavy tails or a sharp peak — energy concentrated in few bins — while low kurtosis indicates a flatter, more uniform energy distribution across the band. The speech signal is the acoustic waveform generated by the speech production system, consisting of the pressure variations radiated from the mouth and nose over time. A gammatone-filter is a human-made linear time-invariant filter whose impulse response is an exponentially-modulated sinusoid — a gamma-shaped envelope h(t)=t^n·e^(−αt)·cos(2πf_c·t + φ) for t≥0 — that models the frequency selectivity of the auditory periphery. It is typically realized as a cascade of four second-order resonator (complex-pole) sections, each tuned to a center frequency f_c, where the decay rate α and the resonance Q set the bandwidth (commonly mapped to the equivalent rectangular bandwidth, ERB). Parameters: (1) center frequency f_c; (2) bandwidth/selectivity (ERB or Q), which sets the decay rate α and the resonator pole placement; (3) the envelope order n and the modulation phase φ; (4) the number of cascade sections (classically four). Persistence mechanism: it persists as a standard mathematical model — the closed-form impulse response plus the resonator-section difference equations — carried in auditory-modeling and audio-analysis literature (the classic gammatone and gammatone-filter-bank toolkits in MATLAB/Python, e.g. the Cochlea and gammatone libraries) and reused as a transform in cochlear and speech-processing front-ends. Boundary: it is a dynamic, time-domain resonator whose output is a decaying oscillation, not the static triangular mel-filter-bank that multiplies a power spectrum by fixed mel-spaced weights. [formal: resonantia gamma-soni | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Parameters: (1) the band's lower and upper frequency bounds, (2) the spectral energy values across frequency bins within the band. Computed as Σ(fᵢ × Eᵢ) / Σ(Eᵢ) where fᵢ is the frequency of bin i and Eᵢ is the spectral energy at that bin — a weighted mean frequency where weights are the per-bin energy values. Indicates whether energy in a band is concentrated toward lower or higher frequencies. Displayed as a scalar time series over analysis frames. Excitation signal is the residual waveform obtained by applying inverse filtering to an observed signal x(n) through an estimated transfer function H(z), yielding the estimated input e(n) = x(n) * H_inv(z) where H_inv(z) = 1/H(z). Parameters: (1) the input signal x(n) — the observed output of the system, (2) the transfer function H(z) to remove — typically a linear-prediction all-pole model or measured frequency response, (3) the inverse filter H_inv(z) — the reciprocal of H(z), implemented as an all-pole filter. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation in DSP software (Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documentation in signal processing literature, and standardized use in source-filter separation, speech analysis, and acoustic modeling. The electroglottogram is the demodulated envelope of the electroglottographic (EGG) voltage waveform. EGG passes a small alternating current through the vocal folds and records the voltage across them; because glottal contact area modulates vocal-fold impedance — high impedance when the glottis is open, low impedance when the folds are in contact — the peak-to-peak voltage amplitude is inversely proportional to glottal contact area. Demodulating the per-cycle peak-to-peak voltage produces a continuous time series whose amplitude is inversely proportional to glottal contact area, tracking the open/close cycle of the glottis. Parameters: (1) the excitation current — a small AC current kept below the safety threshold (typically ~0.5 mA peak at ~2.5 kHz); (2) electrode placement — two submental/neck electrodes completing the current path through the larynx; (3) demodulation — per-cycle peak-to-peak voltage measurement producing a continuous signal. An equivalent-rectangular-bandwidth (ERB) is a human-made, frequency-dependent unit of filter bandwidth used to describe the frequency selectivity of the auditory periphery. Parameters: (1) the center frequency f (kHz); (2) the chosen fitting curve — the Glasberg & Moore (1990) expression is canonical, with alternative fits in the literature. The glottal area function A(t) is a voice-quality measurement construct quantifying the time-varying cross-sectional area of the glottal aperture as a function of time within the glottal cycle: the geometric area of the glottal gap A(t) between the vocal folds, normalized to the cycle's maximum area A_max, reported per cycle and aggregated over voiced frames. Spectral-spread is a spectral analysis parameter quantifying the dispersion of spectral energy across the frequency bins of a full spectrum at a given analysis frame, unbounded by any sub-band. Parameters: (1) the full set of frequency bins i=1..N with center frequencies f_i, (2) the per-bin energy values E_i = |X[k_i]|^2 over the whole spectrum, (3) the analysis frame window. The value is in hertz: a large spread means energy is dispersed across the spectrum, a small spread means energy is concentrated near the centroid. Persistence: the matrix values are the squared magnitudes accumulated per bark bin, stored as a sequence of N×T matrices. Display: a heatmap with time on the x-axis, Bark units on the y-axis, color representing log-energy.

The glottal cycle is the periodic open/close cycle of the glottis during voiced phonation, comprising the opening phase (glottal opening from closed to open), the closed phase (vocal folds in contact), and the transition phases (closing and opening). It is measured per pitch period from the glottal-flow waveform or the electroglottogram envelope. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0, the glottal cycle is partitioned into phases: opening (from the flow maximum to the minimum), closed (the flow at or near zero), and closing (from the minimum back to the maximum). Its parameters include the open quotient (ratio of open-phase duration to the period), the contact quotient (from the electroglottogram envelope), the asymmetry coefficient (ratio of open-phase to close-phase duration), and the return phase (time from flow maximum to return to baseline). Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software from the glottogram and electroglottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: cyclus glottis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Laryngeal-denervation is the human-authored diagnostic concept mapping the loss of motor nerve supply to the intrinsic laryngeal muscles, classifying denervation by the affected nerve branch and its resulting functional deficit. Parameters: (1) the nerve territories - recurrent laryngeal nerve (innervating all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid, causing the affected fold to rest in paramedian position) and superior laryngeal nerve (innervating cricothyroid only, causing pitch range narrowing and voice fatigue); (2) the staging - acute denervation with fibrillation potentials on laryngeal EMG, early reinnervation with polyphasic motor unit potentials, and chronic denervation with permanent paralysis and fibrosis; (3) the etiologies - thyroid surgery (most common iatrogenic cause), endotracheal intubation, cervical trauma, tumor invasion, and post-infectious neuritis; (4) the functional assessment - videostroboscopic mobility grading, acoustic measures (jitter, shimmer, harmonics-to-noise ratio), and laryngeal EMG for denervation/reinnervation classification. Hammarberg index is a voice-quality measure quantifying the ratio of mean subglottal pressure to mean flow during phonation, used as an estimate of glottal adduction efficiency. Computed as the ratio of mean subglottal pressure (measured via occlusion pressure or esophageal balloon) to mean peak-to-peak glottal flow (measured via pneumotachograph or inverse filtering of the acoustic signal). The formula is HI = Psub / Fflow, where Psub is mean subglottal pressure in cmH2O and Fflow is mean airflow in L/s during sustained vowel phonation. Parameters: (1) the subglottal pressure measurement method — occlusion pressure (valsalva maneuver) or esophageal balloon, (2) the airflow measurement method — pneumotachograph or inverse-filtering estimate, (3) the phonation task — typically sustained /a/ at comfortable pitch and loudness. A higher HI indicates greater subglottal pressure for a given flow, suggesting incomplete glottal closure (breathy phonation) or compensatory effort; a lower HI indicates efficient glottal closure. Persistence mechanism: the standardized index documented in laryngology literature, implemented in voice-laboratory measurement protocols, and maintained alongside other glottal efficiency measures. e.g.: Hammarberg index measured from a sustained /a/ in a laryngeal muscle-tension dysphonia study; Hammarberg index reported in a laryngology case series on vocal fold paralysis; Hammarberg index used as a treatment-outcome measure in a voice-therapy protocol | not: phonation-threshold-pressure (the minimum pressure needed to initiate phonation, not a ratio during phonation); glottal-efficiency-index (a related but distinct composite measure) [formal: index Hammarberg | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes]

The cricoid cartilage is the human-authored anatomical construct identifying the complete ring-shaped cartilage forming the inferior-most component of the laryngeal framework, whose posterior lamina is taller than the anterior arch and whose articular facets receive the arytenoid cartilages superiorly. Cepstral-mean-variance normalization (CMVN) is a signal processing technique that normalizes cepstral coefficient vectors by computing the mean and variance across an utterance (or a sliding window) and applying z-score normalization to each frame. Parameters: (1) the mean is computed per coefficient dimension across all frames, (2) the variance is computed per coefficient dimension across all frames, (3) the normalization is applied element-wise as (c_i - μ_i) / σ_i for each coefficient c_i, where σ_i is the standard deviation. The technique removes both channel-induced mean shifts and variance mismatches between speakers. Persistence mechanism: implemented as a standard preprocessing step in speech recognition pipelines (Kaldi, HTK) and encoded in audio processing libraries (Python, MATLAB). The phonation threshold pressure (PTP) is a laryngeal voice-quality parameter quantifying the minimum subglottal pressure at which vocal-fold vibration begins. It is measured by ramping the subglottal pressure (or driving flow) upward through a pressure transducer — a catheter below the glottis in vivo, or a pressure line in an excised-laryx or in-vitro laryx rig — and reading the pressure value at the onset of sustained vocal-fold oscillation, reported in cmH2O or kPa. A high PTP indicates increased vocal-fold load or stiffness (hyperfunctional phonation, edema, paresis with compensatory effort); a low PTP indicates low fold tension or hypofunction. Its parameters are: (1) the measurement setup — in-vivo catheter, excised-laryx rig, or in-vitro laryx model; (2) the pressure ramp rate and the threshold criterion (first sustained oscillation of the glottal flow or fold vibration); (3) the vocal-fold state (tension, adduction, mass) the ramp is applied to; (4) the pressure reference and reporting unit. It is distinct from the subglottal pressure SGP, which is the steady-state or cycle-averaged pressure measured during ongoing phonation, while PTP is the threshold at the onset of phonation. It persists as a standardized clinical and experimental parameter documented in laryngology and voice-surgery literature, and maintained as a member of the voice-quality measurement map. e.g.: phonation threshold pressure measured by a pressure ramp in an excised-laryx study of vocal-fold stiffness; phonation threshold pressure reported in a cadaveric larynx biomechanics study comparing fold tension levels; phonation threshold pressure recorded in an in-vivo laryngeal-effort assessment using a nasotracheal catheter | not: subglottal pressure SGP (the steady-state pressure during ongoing phonation, not the onset threshold); glottal flow waveform g(t) (the output of phonation, not its onset pressure); sound-pressure level at the glottis [formal: limen pressio subglottalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes]

A transfer function is the representation of a linear time-invariant system as the ratio of the transform of its output to the transform of its input with zero initial conditions: H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) in the Laplace domain for continuous-time systems, H(z) = Y(z)/X(z) in the Z domain for discrete-time systems. Parameters: (1) the LTI system whose input-output relation is mapped, (2) the complex domain of the representation (s or z), (3) the numerator and denominator polynomials, whose roots place the system's zeros and poles. The function persists through mathematical notation in control and signal-processing textbooks, engineering standards, and reproducible implementations; engineers use it to analyze stability, predict frequency response, and design controllers and filters. [formal: functio transferens | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The spectral centroid is a human-made measure used in signal and audio processing that quantifies the center of mass of a spectrum's magnitude distribution — the point at which the energy of the spectrum would balance if it were a physical object. It is computed as the weighted mean of the frequency components, where the weights are the magnitudes at each frequency, and is typically expressed in Hertz. The spectral centroid serves as a proxy for the perceptual attribute of brightness in sound, since higher centroids correspond to more high-frequency energy. It is a scalar descriptor extracted from a single spectrum frame and is widely used in audio analysis, instrument recognition, and music information retrieval. e.g.: spectral centroid of a musical note computed by a Short-Time Fourier Transform; spectral centroid used to distinguish bass from treble timbre in a music information retrieval study; spectral centroid of a speech formant band measured in Praat for voice quality analysis | not: spectral-band-centroid (a centroid computed within a sub-band, not the full spectrum) [formal: centrum spectrale | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

The root mean square energy within a defined frequency sub-band: the square root of the mean of squared energy values across all per-bin energy bins within the band. Persistence: a scalar time series over analysis frames, used as a band-local energy measure in audio analysis toolkits. e.g.: RMS energy in the 300-3400 Hz speech band used for voiced/unvoiced decision in Praat; RMS energy of the low-frequency band applied in drum sound classification; RMS energy of a 1000-5000 Hz band measured for voice quality screening [formal: vis quadrata media | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes]

Derivation is a human-made morphological operation — the process by which a language creates a new lexeme from an existing one by adding derivational material. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) lexeme change: the output is a new lexeme with a distinct dictionary identity from the input (happy → happiness is one lexeme becoming another; walk → walked is NOT derivation, because walked is an inflected form of the same lexeme as walk). This lexeme-change criterion is the decisive boundary from inflection. (2) derivational material: the operation is carried by a bound morpheme (affix) or, in some languages, by a change of stress, vowel, or other internal modification that contributes derivational meaning (English sing → song: an ablaut-derived noun; by contrast the tense forms sang and sung remain inflected forms of the same lexeme as sing). (3) conventionalized meaning: the derivational material contributes a systematic, predictable meaning (-ness 'state of being', un- 'negation', -er 'agent') that transforms the input lexeme's meaning in a rule-governed way. Paradigmatic cases: happy + -ness → happiness (new lexeme); write → writer (new lexeme, agentive). Derivation persists as a productive rule — speakers coin new derived lexemes on the fly — and as a stable category of grammatical description: derivational affixes are catalogued in the morphological inventory of each language. [formal: derivatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]
